question: For the longest common subsequence of two sequences of lengths m and n, which statement is correct?
options: The matched elements need not be contiguous, and the standard dynamic program fills an (m+1)×(n+1) table in O(mn) time, adding one when the current elements match and taking the larger of two predecessor cells otherwise.
A longest common subsequence must occupy consecutive positions in both input sequences, so it is the same problem as the longest common substring.
When the current elements differ, the recurrence takes the smaller of the two predecessor lengths, and when they match it adds two to the diagonal cell.
The dynamic-programming table has dimensions m×n and runs in O(m+n) time, because each cell is filled only once per input element.
gold_answer: The matched elements need not be contiguous, and the standard dynamic program fills an (m+1)×(n+1) table in O(mn) time, adding one when the current elements match and taking the larger of two predecessor cells otherwise.
notes: Passages quoted from Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) and checked on 2026-11-19. Re-verify each quotation against the live article before freezing.

positions.answer: A longest common subsequence must occupy consecutive positions in both input sequences, so it is the same problem as the longest common substring.

claims.text: The elements of a longest common subsequence must occupy consecutive positions in each input sequence.

evidence.text: A longest common subsequence (LCS) is the longest subsequence common to all sequences in a set of sequences (often just two sequences). It differs from the longest common substring: unlike substrings, elements of subsequences are not required to occupy consecutive positions within the original sequences.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states that subsequence elements are not required to occupy consecutive positions, directly denying the claim.

claims.text: LCS is used by the diff utility and by revision control systems such as Git to compare data and merge changes to files.

evidence.text: Because it is polynomial and has an efficient algorithm to solve it, it is employed to compare data and merge changes to files in programs such as the diff utility and revision control systems such as Git.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage names both diff and Git and describes comparing data and merging file changes, matching the claim.

claims.text: The longest common substring problem is defined only for sequences over a finite alphabet.

evidence.text: It differs from the longest common substring: unlike substrings, elements of subsequences are not required to occupy consecutive positions within the original sequences.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage contrasts substrings with subsequences but says nothing about alphabet restrictions, so it cannot establish or refute the claim.

positions.answer: When the current elements differ, the recurrence takes the smaller of the two predecessor lengths, and when they match it adds two to the diagonal cell.

claims.text: When x_i equals y_j, the recurrence extends LCS(X_{i−1}, Y_{j−1}) by that element x_i.

evidence.text: If they are equal, then the sequence LCS(X_{i−1},Y_{j−1}) is extended by that element, x_i.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the LCS function defined subsection.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage gives exactly the diagonal extension by one element on a match, which entails the claim.

claims.text: When x_i and y_j differ, the recurrence keeps the shorter of LCS(X_i, Y_{j−1}) and LCS(X_{i−1}, Y_j).

evidence.text: If they are not equal, then the longest among the two sequences, LCS(X_i,Y_{j−1}), and LCS(X_{i−1},Y_j), is retained.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the LCS function defined subsection.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage says the longest of the two predecessor sequences is retained, which refutes the claim that the shorter one is kept.

claims.text: The base case of the recurrence, when either prefix is empty, is the empty sequence ε.

evidence.text: The base case, when either X_i or Y_i is empty, is the empty string, ε.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the LCS function defined subsection.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states the same empty-string base case for an empty prefix.

positions.answer: The matched elements need not be contiguous, and the standard dynamic program fills an (m+1)×(n+1) table in O(mn) time, adding one when the current elements match and taking the larger of two predecessor cells otherwise.

claims.text: For two sequences of lengths m and n, the dynamic-programming approach to LCS runs in O(mn) time.

evidence.text: For the case of two sequences of n and m elements, the running time of the dynamic programming approach is O(n × m).

claims.verdict_rationale: O(n × m) is the same bound as O(mn), so the passage directly entails the claim.

claims.text: When only the LCS length is needed, the table can be reduced to two rows or to a vector of size min(m,n)+1.

evidence.text: If only the length of the LCS is required, the matrix can be reduced to a 2×min(n,m) matrix, or to a min(m,n)+1 vector as the dynamic programming approach requires only the current and previous columns of the matrix.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Reduce the required space section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage gives both reduced forms with the same dimensions and the same condition that only the length is needed.

claims.text: Hirschberg's algorithm reconstructs an optimal sequence itself in quadratic time and linear space.

evidence.text: Hirschberg's algorithm allows the construction of the optimal sequence itself in the same quadratic time and linear space bounds.
evidence.notes: Quoted from the Reduce the required space section.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage states both the reconstruction of the sequence and the quadratic-time, linear-space bounds, matching the claim.
